### Preserve the assigned configuration across a task

A canary is live execution, not a shadow with its output exposed. Before assigning tasks, declare the eligible population, allocation rule, candidate configuration, comparison policy, resource limits, and stop conditions. A configuration includes the relevant model request, prompt, tools, harness, and verifier versions. An allocation fraction limits the share assigned under that rule; it is neither a per-task authority grant nor a worst-case bound on total effects.

Assign the configuration at the task or trajectory boundary and preserve that assignment through its continuation. Per-model-call routing could mix baseline and candidate behavior within one measured task, so neither configuration's result would be identified cleanly. Retries, resumed work, and delayed labels must retain the original cohort identity. If a customer or repository creates dependent tasks, the randomization and analysis may need that larger unit rather than treating each call as an independent trial.

This is **trajectory-level sticky routing**, a stable configuration assignment rather than a promise to retain one physical model instance. Workers can change under @sec-vol3-persistence-migration. Continuation requires compatible recorded state, current ownership, and an explicit decision about configuration changes. Cache reuse follows its own compatibility and availability contract; cohort assignment alone does not guarantee warm serving state. Record the provenance actually exposed by the serving interface rather than treating a model label as proof of unchanged internals.

Outcome delay matters even when assignment is correct. Keep every admitted task in its cohort ledger, with pass, fail, pending, or unknown verdict and the observation cutoff. Counting only completed fast tasks can make a slow failing candidate look favorable. The analysis must specify when labels are considered mature, how unresolved cases affect promotion, and which time and resource endpoints it measures. A failed label-delivery path is an evidence failure, not a reason to remove those tasks from the denominator.

### Monitor a specified sequential alternative

A planned fixed-sample comparison remains valid when its assumptions hold. Repeatedly applying that test after each new outcome generally changes its error behavior. A sequential design instead declares how accumulating evidence will be used before observing it. The sequential probability ratio test (SPRT) provides a compact example for two specified distributions; it is not the paired offline noninferiority procedure used earlier.

For this local model, let independent task labels $x_i$ be Bernoulli with a stationary acceptance probability. The simple hypotheses specify $p=p_0$ and $p=p_1$, where $0<p_1<p_0<1$ and the lower value represents a particular degradation. Both values are design inputs, not a claim that an estimated historical baseline is known exactly. With $d_n=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$, the log-likelihood ratio favoring the degraded hypothesis is

$$\Lambda_n = d_n \ln\left(\frac{p_1}{p_0}\right) + (n-d_n)\ln\left(\frac{1-p_1}{1-p_0}\right).$$ {#eq-vol3-release-sprt}

Success moves the statistic in @eq-vol3-release-sprt downward; failure moves it upward. Let $\alpha$ target the probability of choosing degradation under $p_0$, and $\beta$ the probability of choosing $p_0$ under $p_1$. For $0<\alpha,\beta<1$ and $\alpha+\beta<1$, Wald's commonly used approximate log boundaries are

$$u = \ln\left(\frac{1-\beta}{\alpha}\right), \qquad \ell = \ln\left(\frac{\beta}{1-\alpha}\right).$$ {#eq-vol3-release-sprt-boundaries}

These are approximate thresholds. Discrete observations can overshoot them, so they do not individually guarantee the requested error probabilities without further calibration. [Fischer and Ramdas](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.16076v1) explain this distinction for the approximate SPRT. A release implementation must validate the selected boundaries and decision protocol for its actual statistical model.

::: {#not-13-sprt-circuit-breaker .callout-note title="What a sequential decision supports"}

At $\Lambda_n\ge u$, the test selects the specified degraded hypothesis and the release policy can stop new candidate admission. At $\Lambda_n\le\ell$, it selects $p_0$ against that particular alternative. Between the boundaries, evidence remains inconclusive. Selecting $p_0$ does not establish general noninferiority, authorize broader traffic, or prove safety. A deadline or maximum sample allowance can also end collection inconclusively; it must not be converted into a favorable decision.

:::

A production stream can violate this model through changing task mix, shared outages, correlated repository tasks, or delayed labels. Processing results in completion order can create selection bias when duration depends on outcome. A declared admission-order analysis with mature labels avoids that particular reordering, but can wait behind an unresolved task. Another valid design may model delayed outcomes explicitly. In either case, unknowns cannot silently become passes or disappear. Testing several metrics or restarting a test after an unfavorable path also requires an error-control protocol beyond these two boundaries.

The same simplified model gives a planning approximation for the expected stopping sample count. Under $p_1$, the expected increment is $m_1=p_1\ln(p_1/p_0)+(1-p_1)\ln((1-p_1)/(1-p_0))$. Neglecting boundary overshoot and substituting the target decision probabilities gives

$$\mathbb{E}_1[N]\approx\frac{(1-\beta)u+\beta\ell}{m_1}.$$ {#eq-vol3-release-sprt-samples}

The numerator in @eq-vol3-release-sprt-samples averages both terminal decisions, as in the stopping-sample approximation in [Hory and Hero, Equation 24](https://arxiv.org/pdf/quant-ph/0402181). Consequently, this expression estimates time to a decision in sample units, not time to successful detection conditional on an alarm. Its approximations must remain visible when converting samples into an operational timeline. @Sec-vol3-appendix-math-sprt derives the approximate decision boundaries and stopping-sample expression while distinguishing target errors from realized errors.

```{python}
#| label: lego-13-sizing-canary-traffic-and-circuit
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SEQUENTIAL STOPPING SCALE, NOT A HARM BOUND
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-13-sizing-canary-traffic-and-circuit in sec-vol3-evaluation-releases.
# │ Goal: Compute Wald's no-overshoot stopping approximation and label-time scale.
# │ Show: Boundaries, drift, approximate sample count, and delayed calendar time.
# │ How: Hypothetical stationary Bernoulli model with regular admissions.
# │ Note: Separate later configuration; no promotion of the inconclusive pair.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from math import log
from mlsysim import *

class SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker:
    # 1. LOAD: hypothetical monitor inputs, not production measurements.
    p0, p1 = 0.90, 0.75
    alpha, beta = 0.01, 0.05
    arrival_per_hr = 60
    fraction = 0.05
    label_delay = 0.5 * hour

    # 2. EXECUTE: approximate boundary mixture includes BOTH decisions.
    upper = log((1 - beta) / alpha)
    lower = log(beta / (1 - alpha))
    drift = p1 * log(p1 / p0) + (1 - p1) * log((1 - p1) / (1 - p0))
    expected_terminal = (1 - beta) * upper + beta * lower
    expected_samples = expected_terminal / drift
    canary_per_hr = arrival_per_hr * fraction
    sampling_time = expected_samples / canary_per_hr * hour
    label_time = sampling_time + label_delay

    # 3. GUARD: numerical scale and distinction between samples and time.
    check(0 < p1 < p0 < 1, "Specified degraded Bernoulli alternative")
    check(abs(upper - 4.5538768916) < 1e-9, "Upper approximate log boundary")
    check(abs(lower + 2.9856819377) < 1e-9, "Lower approximate log boundary")
    check(45.23 < expected_samples < 45.24, "No-overshoot stopping approximation")
    check(canary_per_hr == 3, "Assigned arrival rate")
    check(abs(label_time.to(hour).magnitude - 15.5793544806) < 1e-9, "Regular arrivals plus fixed label delay")
    check(label_time > sampling_time, "Labels arrive after admission")

    # 4. OUTPUT: every export is consumed in the notebook below.
    p0_str, p1_str = fmt(p0, precision=2), fmt(p1, precision=2)
    alpha_str, beta_str = fmt(alpha, precision=2), fmt(beta, precision=2)
    arrivals_str = fmt_int(arrival_per_hr)
    fraction_pct_str = fmt_percent(fraction, precision=0, style="prose")
    delay_str = fmt_qty(label_delay, hour, precision=1)
    upper_str, lower_str = fmt(upper, precision=4), fmt(lower, precision=4)
    drift_str = fmt(drift, precision=5)
    terminal_str = fmt(expected_terminal, precision=4)
    samples_str = fmt(expected_samples, precision=2)
    canary_arrivals_str = fmt_int(canary_per_hr)
    sampling_time_str = fmt_qty(sampling_time, hour, precision=2)
    label_time_str = fmt_qty(label_time, hour, precision=2)
```

::: {#nbk-13-sizing-canary-traffic-and-circuit .callout-notebook title="Sequential evidence takes calendar time"}

**Problem**: Consider a separate, hypothetical later configuration that has met its offline and shadow prerequisites. Its monitor compares $p_0$ equal to `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.p0_str` with $p_1$ equal to `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.p1_str`, using design targets $\alpha$ equal to `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.alpha_str` and $\beta$ equal to `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.beta_str`. At `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.arrivals_str` eligible tasks/hour and a `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.fraction_pct_str` candidate allocation, what stopping-sample and calendar-time scale does the no-overshoot approximation predict under $p_1$?

**Assumptions**: The task outcomes are independent with the stated constant probability. Candidate admissions occur at regular intervals, with the first admission after one interval. Each label becomes available exactly `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.delay_str` after admission, independently of its value. No labels are lost. This planning calculation models an untruncated test with no operational tripwire; real deployment limits can stop collection earlier and change its stopping distribution.

**Calculation**: The approximate boundaries are `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.upper_str` and `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.lower_str`. Under $p_1$, the expected increment is `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.drift_str`. Neglecting overshoot and substituting the target decision probabilities gives expected terminal log-likelihood `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.terminal_str`. Dividing that quantity by the expected increment gives approximately `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.samples_str` labeled tasks. The average includes both possible decisions, including mistaken selection of $p_0$; it is not the expected number until an alarm.

Candidate admissions occur at `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.canary_arrivals_str` tasks/hour. The corresponding admission-time scale is `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.sampling_time_str`; adding the fixed label delay gives approximately `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.label_time_str` until a decision. Tasks admitted while labels are pending can still be executing when the test stops. Variable completion times, missing labels, or a different arrival process require a different calendar-time model.

**Systems insight**: A small allocation can reduce admitted exposure over a fixed interval while slowing evidence collection. The expected sample count is not a maximum, the approximation is not an exact operating characteristic, and neither bounds harmful effects. The release policy needs independent admission and effect limits even when the statistical monitor is correctly implemented.

:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-evaluation-canary-excess-failures
#| echo: false
# WHICH HARM THE CANARY FRACTION CONTROLS (LEGO)
# Goal: Separate excess failures from a measured regression from exposure rate.
# Scope: Same hypothetical monitor as the sequential-evidence notebook, under p1.
from mlsysim import hour
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check

class CanaryExcessFailures:
    # 1. LOAD: reuse the monitor's design inputs; compare with full allocation.
    m = SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker
    full_fraction = 1.0

    # 2. EXECUTE: tasks admitted by the decision = labeled samples + admitted during label delay.
    gap = m.p0 - m.p1
    delay_hr = m.label_delay.to(hour).magnitude
    pending_canary = m.arrival_per_hr * m.fraction * delay_hr
    pending_full = m.arrival_per_hr * full_fraction * delay_hr
    excess_canary = (m.expected_samples + pending_canary) * gap
    excess_full = (m.expected_samples + pending_full) * gap
    exposure_ratio = full_fraction / m.fraction

    # 3. GUARD: the fraction enters only through the label delay.
    check(abs(pending_canary - 1.5) < 1e-9 and abs(pending_full - 30) < 1e-9, "Tasks admitted while labels pend")
    check(6.9 < excess_canary < 7.1, "Excess failures at the canary fraction")
    check(11.2 < excess_full < 11.4, "Excess failures at full allocation")
    check(abs(exposure_ratio - 20) < 1e-9, "Admission-rate ratio")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    excess_canary_str = fmt_int(round(excess_canary))
    excess_full_str = fmt_int(round(excess_full))
```

The sample count and the canary fraction control different harms. Under $p_1$, each candidate task fails about $p_0-p_1$ more often than it would under the baseline. With allocation fraction $\rho$ of eligible arrivals at rate $\lambda$ and label delay $d$, the monitor decides after roughly $\mathbb{E}_1[N]$ labeled tasks plus the $\rho\lambda d$ tasks admitted while their labels are pending, so the measured regression costs about $(\mathbb{E}_1[N]+\rho\lambda d)(p_0-p_1)$ excess failures. In the notebook's scenario that is about `{python} CanaryExcessFailures.excess_canary_str` at the canary fraction and about `{python} CanaryExcessFailures.excess_full_str` at full allocation. The fraction enters only through the label delay; its main effect on a measured regression is the calendar time needed to collect the samples. Harms the monitor does not measure behave differently. They accrue for every admitted candidate task until some other mechanism detects them, so their rate scales with $\rho$, and this canary exposes candidate tasks at `{python} SizingCanaryTrafficCircuitBreaker.fraction_pct_str` of the full-allocation rate. The test's sample size fixes the harm from a measured regression; the canary's size limits the harms the test does not measure.

### Stop admission without erasing outstanding work

A hard operational tripwire does not wait for enough statistical evidence. A verified forbidden dispatch, exhausted release allowance, or exceeded limit on unresolved candidate work can stop further admission under the declared policy. Task-level reservations and finalization remain governed by @sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting. A task-count cap can bound effects only when each task's relevant effects are also bounded at enforcing endpoints; a routing percentage alone supplies neither bound.

Rollback changes which configuration may receive new work. It does not retract transmitted requests, restore every changed object, or automatically make a baseline worker eligible to continue a candidate trajectory. Record the hold at the admission boundaries, track their confirmed enforcement, and retain outstanding candidate operations under their original identities. A supported cancellation may stop some work; uncertain cancellation remains unresolved. Any continuation under another configuration needs the ownership and compatibility checks from @sec-vol3-persistence-migration.

The recovery policy from @sec-vol3-failure-recovery governs established effects, registered cleanup, commitments, and residual owners. Its separately bounded administrative cleanup can remain necessary after candidate routing stops. Measure detection, confirmed admission stop, and effect settlement as distinct intervals. Some effects cannot be undone, and some outcomes remain unknown at the reporting cutoff; neither belongs in an average that implies every case was restored.

### Count accepted work over the observed interval

Release reporting must preserve the distinction between a fraction of tasks, a rate of completion, and the resources spent producing them. The accepted task is the unit that trajectory goodput (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-goodput}) charges all initiated work against, so the release record counts it the same way. For a declared admitted cohort of size $N$, let $N_{\text{accepted}}$ count tasks meeting the complete acceptance contract by the observation cutoff. Then $q_{\text{observed}}=N_{\text{accepted}}/N$ counts observed accepted tasks without dropping pending or unknown cases. Report their separate counts; this is not an estimate of eventual acceptance obtained by pretending every unresolved task failed permanently.

For an observation interval $[t_a,t_b)$, let $N_{\text{accepted}}[t_a,t_b)$ count acceptance events in that interval under the declared measurement policy. Verified throughput is

$$\Theta = \frac{N_{\text{accepted}}[t_a,t_b)}{t_b-t_a}.$$

The denominator is elapsed observation time, not the sum of overlapping task durations. State the interval's startup and drain treatment, concurrency, arrival policy, resource allocation, and whether tasks began before the interval. A small canary that receives little work can be arrival-limited; its raw throughput is not directly comparable with a fully loaded baseline's capacity.

@Tbl-vol3-sre-metrics keeps companion measurements tied to their denominators. These signals explain a release decision without replacing the acceptance comparison.

| Measurement                | Denominator or boundary                                                                                   | Interpretation to preserve                                                                    |
|:---------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Observed accepted fraction | All tasks in the declared admitted cohort                                                                 | Report failed, pending, and unknown cases separately                                          |
| Verified throughput        | Elapsed observation interval                                                                              | Match workload and capacity before comparing rates                                            |
| Cost per accepted task     | Accepted count, with all included cohort costs in the numerator                                           | Include failed work and report unsettled liability; undefined when none are accepted          |
| Intervention burden        | Events per task, or tasks with an intervention divided by all tasks                                       | Event counts can exceed one per task; routine required approval is not automatically a defect |
| Latency and settlement     | Named start/end events and observation cutoff                                                             | Report unresolved cases; an empirical percentile is not a hard per-task deadline              |
| Behavioral change          | Comparable input mix and declared action-counting policy; $D_{\mathrm{JS}}$ from @eq-vol3-eval-tool-drift | A different tool distribution may reflect improvement, regression, or changed demand          |

: **Release measurements and their scope**: Operational signals retain their units and populations. Zero observed violations does not establish zero future risk, and a denied proposal is distinct from an escaped effect. {#tbl-vol3-sre-metrics}

Staged release connects evidence to a bounded next decision while leaving uncertainty visible. The paired comparison, diagnostic experiment, and sequential monitor answer different questions and cannot substitute for one another. A coherent release record brings those results together with their fixtures, limits, and residual obligations so that the resulting decision can be inspected.

## An Evidence-Backed Evaluation Decision {#sec-vol3-evaluation-synthesis}

`candidate_v2` accepts more tasks than `baseline_v1` in the paired sample, and a separate diagnostic experiment suggests a useful interface repair. Neither result, by itself, clears the release rule. We can now assemble the evidence to distinguish what is ready, what remains unresolved, and which next experiment is justified.

### Assemble the decision record {#sec-vol3-evaluation-synthesis-architecture}

@Tbl-vol3-controlplane-layers brings together the chapter's hypothetical trial, paired comparison, and diagnostic experiment. The pending repair trial remains outside the comparison's prespecified cohort; its missing result was not selectively excluded. The record preserves each experiment's identity so that a useful finding cannot silently become evidence for a different claim.

| Evidence record field           | Entry or required reference                                                                                                                   | Decision consequence                                                                                                                                                                           |
|:--------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Task, fixture, and criteria     | `pool_repair_01`, `pool_fixture_v1`, `repair_accept_v1`; record permitted effects, required checks, budgets, and residual-duty conditions     | The verdict concerns this declared task contract, not unrestricted correctness.                                                                                                                |
| Trial and artifact identity     | `eval_pool_01_candidate_v2_run1`, configuration `candidate_v2`, artifact `ws_r19`; preserve grader and check versions                         | Do not confuse a trial, system configuration, source artifact, or historical operation.                                                                                                        |
| Individual trial verdict        | Targeted check passed; required regression evidence remains pending in the opening worksheet                                                  | Do not accept the trial merely because one check passed. Preserve other established failures or unknowns independently.                                                                        |
| Paired comparison               | The complete task-pair record and candidate-minus-baseline interval from @sec-vol3-evaluation-rigor, with its prespecified degradation margin | The worked comparison does not establish noninferiority; favorable marginal counts do not override that result.                                                                                |
| Resources and unresolved duties | Account for all started generation, grading, tools, and declared finalization; retain actual charges and outstanding liability separately     | A pending final bill is not zero cost. Whether sufficient bounded evidence satisfies a criterion follows the stated contract.                                                                  |
| Capture and privacy             | Retained trace boundaries, payload availability, sampling probabilities, delayed verdicts, drops, and authorized evidence access              | Diagnostic completeness and population representativeness require evidence; redacted bytes cannot be claimed available for exact replay.                                                       |
| Diagnosis and regression        | `diag_pool_truncation_v1`, the controlled observation-interface experiment, and its fixture-specific regression tests                         | Support a scoped intervention hypothesis without labeling the model or interface the sole possible cause. Its repeated fixture runs are not additional independent tasks in the paired cohort. |
| Release disposition             | Retain the baseline; no live promotion of this candidate on the current evidence                                                              | Further work needs a stated question and planned evidence collection, not an automatic increase in traffic.                                                                                    |

: **An integrated evaluation record**: Each field identifies what the evidence supports and which decision it constrains. Missing or pending evidence remains visible rather than becoming an implicit pass. {#tbl-vol3-controlplane-layers}

The record need not copy sensitive prompts into a broadly accessible report. It can reference protected artifacts and summarize their coverage, while making unavailable material explicit. Nor does it replace the authoritative operation ledger. A late result can update a verdict or settle a charge through its responsible owner without restarting an obsolete continuation. Evaluation records what that evidence changes; it does not erase obligations by relabeling a trial.

### Check whether the evidence answers the question {#sec-vol3-evaluation-synthesis-readiness}

The record exposes different next actions. The individual repair needs its required regression and accounting results. The interface change needs tests beyond its saved diagnostic fixture. The comparative release question needs evidence sufficient for its prespecified margin. Collecting another detailed trace does not answer all three questions; the missing claim determines the next measurement.

Preserve the distinction between collecting more evidence and changing the question. Removing difficult tasks, excluding pending results, enlarging the budget, or changing the selector can raise a reported rate while changing its meaning. A legitimate revision records a new protocol or configuration and evaluates it under the appropriate comparison. It does not retrospectively redefine the original experiment as successful.

### Apply the declared decision rule {#sec-vol3-evaluation-synthesis-math}

The worked paired comparison in @sec-vol3-evaluation-rigor estimates candidate-minus-baseline acceptance, preserving both concordant and discordant task outcomes. Its uncertainty interval extends below the allowed degradation threshold. Under the declared rule, the available evidence therefore does not establish noninferiority. It also does not establish superiority. This conclusion is not a finding that the candidate is certainly worse; it is a limit on what this experiment supports.

Operationally, a declared decision rule is a conjunction of criteria, each tied to its own evidence:

$$G=\mathbf{1}\!\left[L_\Delta>-\delta_{\mathrm{tol}}\right]\wedge
\mathbf{1}\!\left[\Theta_c\ge(1-\epsilon_\Theta)\,\Theta_b\right]\wedge
\mathbf{1}\!\left[\widehat T_{c,0.99}\le T_{\max}\right]\wedge
\mathbf{1}\!\left[V_c=0\right].$$ {#eq-vol3-eval-release-gate}

The first term in @eq-vol3-eval-release-gate is the paired noninferiority criterion. The second compares verified throughput $\Theta$ over matched intervals, workloads, and capacity, within a declared tolerance $\epsilon_\Theta$. The third bounds an empirical high-percentile completion time against a declared ceiling $T_{\max}$; it is an estimate over the cohort, not a per-task deadline. The fourth is different in kind. $V_c$ counts verified forbidden effects, and a single one fails the gate as a hard tripwire; zero observed violations remains an observation, not an estimate of zero risk. A behavioral-drift measure such as @eq-vol3-eval-tool-drift beyond its declared threshold routes the decision to review rather than failing it, because a changed tool distribution can be the intended repair. The conjunction fails when any term fails, so favorable latency, a lower bill, or no observed policy violations cannot substitute for the unmet acceptance-rate requirement. Under this protocol, the disposition remains a hold.

The release decision is to retain `baseline_v1` and withhold live promotion of `candidate_v2`, consistent with @sec-vol3-evaluation-releases. Resolve the individual trial's pending evidence under its observation policy, inspect the diagnostic findings, and plan any further comparative experiment before collecting its confirmatory data. Repeatedly rerunning the same gate until it passes is a different stopping procedure and needs a method that accounts for those repeated looks. The separate sequential-monitoring example describes a later eligible configuration; it does not reverse this candidate's offline result.

An automated gate can enforce this declared policy, but its deterministic execution does not make its statistical premises certain. Report whether each criterion passed, failed, or remains inconclusive, and distinguish hard operational tripwires from estimated population properties. Combining several nominal confidence statements does not automatically supply one confidence level for every claim in the release report. The decision protocol must state which hypotheses, comparisons, and repeated looks its error accounting covers.

::: {.callout-checkpoint title="Defend the evaluation decision"}

- [ ] **Evidence scope**: Why does the targeted pass for `ws_r19` not accept its trial while the required regression result is pending? Why is `test_r18` not a replacement result?
- [ ] **Comparison**: Why can a candidate have more accepted trials in the paired sample without clearing the prespecified noninferiority rule?
- [ ] **Diagnosis**: What does a successful observation-interface intervention on one fixture support, and what broader claim still needs evaluation?
- [ ] **Next step**: Which missing evidence would you collect before reconsidering promotion, and how would you prevent repeated testing or selective exclusions from changing the claimed decision rule?

:::

The useful product of evaluation is this accountable decision: the tested configuration, the evidence and its limits, the permitted next step, and the obligations still open. The following pitfalls expose ways that a superficially complete report can lose those distinctions.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-evaluation-fallacies}

The strongest-looking evaluation report can still answer the wrong question. These mistakes concern the link between evidence and the claim drawn from it.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *A successful check or isolated grader proves the task is correct.*

A check establishes only what its criteria and measurement cover. Isolation can protect the grader from some interference without making its specification complete or its execution immune to malicious candidate code. Task acceptance requires the declared outcome, process, resource, and evidence conditions; one targeted pass or a fluent completion claim cannot replace them.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Using uncertainty about two separate rates as uncertainty about their difference.*

Marginal Wilson intervals estimate individual proportions. Their overlap, or a comparison of their lower bounds, is not the paired candidate-minus-baseline test. Preserve task pairing, define the tolerated degradation before inspection, and use the corresponding comparison method. Inconclusive evidence does not establish equivalence, improvement, or certain regression.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *Retaining anomalous traces captures every failure and gives a representative sample.*

Some task failures appear only after a delayed verdict, and finite buffers or missing instrumentation can lose evidence. Anomaly enrichment also changes inclusion probabilities. Report capture limits and denominators, preserve appropriate representative samples, and keep recovery-required records separate from optional diagnostics. A redaction policy narrows accessible detail rather than guaranteeing both complete privacy and exact replay.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Treating one successful intervention or release test as a universal guarantee.*

A controlled intervention supports a conclusion under its fixture and experimental assumptions; it need not identify a sole cause. A release gate supports its declared decision, not absence of every unmeasured harm. Retain regression tests, bounded exposure, delayed-outcome accounting, and recovery owners. Stopping new candidate traffic does not undo effects already started.
:::

## Summary {#sec-vol3-evaluation-summary}

The runtime can enforce admission, preserve a history, and recover partial effects without knowing whether the task was completed. Evaluation supplies a declared acceptance contract and evidence for judging it. In the repair, a candidate-specific targeted pass, a pending regression result, and a reserved but unsettled charge remain different facts. The evaluator must preserve their meanings rather than collapse them into a success label.

Comparable fixtures and protected grading make trials interpretable. Sampling and paired comparisons then determine what their outcomes support about a system configuration. Traces expose recorded timing and dependencies; retention and privacy policies determine which evidence remains available. Controlled interventions test explanations, and staged release policies govern what may happen next. The worked comparison ends without promotion because its evidence does not meet the declared rule, even though the candidate's observed acceptance count is higher.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Match every evaluation claim to its evidence"}

* **Define acceptance before counting success**: Specify required outcomes, process and authority conditions, resource limits, and evidence sufficiency. Read-only tasks can be accepted without a persistent state change. Preserve pass, fail, pending, and unknown verdicts; missing evidence is not a successful check.
* **Make trials comparable and protect grading**: Record task fixtures, system configurations, artifact versions, permitted randomness, and reset assumptions. Separate development feedback from held-out assessment. Protect the grader from both the acting agent and its submitted artifact, while stating fidelity and coverage limits.
* **Calibrate the instrument that supplies each verdict**: Mechanical checks, process assessment, and human or model judgments have different roles and errors. Agreement is not truth. Use representative independently assessed cases, explicit rubrics, and uncertainty; distinguish false acceptance from failure among accepted outputs.
* **Match stochastic metrics to the deployed policy**: Preserve task and run units, task pairing, and the chosen population or fixed-suite estimand. Separate one-rate intervals from comparative inference, potential from repeated consistency, and batch selection from sequential stopping. Count the costs of all started work.
* **Preserve useful evidence within capture and privacy limits**: Correlate task, configuration, artifact, operation, and outcome without mistaking identifiers for authority or causation. Respect overlapping spans when measuring time. Report sampling, delayed verdicts, drops, and unavailable payloads; diagnostic retention cannot replace required recovery history.
* **Test explanations without rewriting the past**: Reconstruction folds records, regression replay exercises logic against captured inputs, and new model calls are experiments. Match observations to their actual requests and versions. Controlled changes support scoped conclusions, while regressions test declared postconditions rather than a convenient status label.
* **Stage exposure under a stated decision protocol**: Offline, shadow, and canary stages answer different questions. Preserve cohort assignment, delayed outcomes, current authority, and hard resource limits. Statistical stopping rules do not bound every harm, and rollback of new routing does not settle outstanding effects.
* **Assemble a decision rather than a favorable scorecard**: Connect criteria, fixtures, graders, paired outcomes, costs, capture limits, diagnosis, and release conditions in one record. Keep unsupported claims inconclusive. Plan the next evidence collection before retesting, and preserve the distinction between acceptance, comparative improvement, and permission to deploy.

:::

Causal and statistical release evidence (principle \ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}) requires the decision to name its task criteria, experimental scope, and uncertainty. Recorded traces and controlled comparisons connect a finding to inspectable evidence without promising complete capture or a unique cause. The resulting gate governs a specified next step; it does not certify every future outcome.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From evaluation evidence to curated trajectories"}

Which of these trajectories should become training data, and which failures call for a change outside the model? @Sec-vol3-trajectory-curation uses evaluation evidence to guide diagnosis, admission, and corpus design. A logged success is not automatically a useful demonstration, and a failure is not automatically a policy defect. Preserve criterion and configuration provenance, unresolved evidence, and the separation between development data and held-out evaluation. Curation turns that qualified record into a learning-data decision, not a promise that training on it will be safe or beneficial.

:::
